issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the validated trauma type of toxic chemical exposure. 'Specific body parts associated with the event,' 'power imbalance,' and 'being alone with women' are much more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual assault formulations than toxic exposure.

issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items point to incompatible trauma meanings: body-part cues, gendered interpersonal cues, and power-over-me situations imply an assaultive perpetrator context rather than an occupational chemical exposure event.

issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a 62-year-old male bomb disposal technician whose index trauma is toxic chemical exposure, 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-related trigger. It implies an interpersonal/sexual-threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the threat items, which instead reflect generalized physical danger/hypervigilance.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure, which typically does not involve an identifiable perpetrator. This item suggests an assault/interpersonal trauma formulation and is inconsistent with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: Avoiding new relationships is hard to reconcile with a 62-year-old married bomb disposal technician whose indexed trauma is toxic chemical exposure; this strategy fits interpersonal trauma or betrayal formulations more than exposure-related PTSD, and there are no corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal items to support an interpersonal-relationship focus.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone in a room or building does not connect well to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe generalized hypervigilance and escape planning, while the trauma type and other selected triggers do not suggest solitary settings as a specific danger cue. This looks like a maladaptive strategy for a symptom pattern not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is difficult to integrate with toxic chemical exposure and the rest of the selected profile. The other triggers are workplace and loud noises, and the threat items reflect environmental danger monitoring rather than coercion or dominance. This trigger suggests an interpersonal/control-based trauma theme that is unsupported elsewhere.

vignette:
# Kofi's Vigilance

Kofi Mensah was forty-eight years old when the incident happened, a man whose steady hands and methodical temperament had made him one of the most respected bomb disposal technicians in his state. He had spent two decades disarming threats with the kind of calm focus that his colleagues relied on—the ability to isolate fear and set it aside while fingers worked with precision through the final seconds before detonation. But on a humid June afternoon in 2010, during a routine sweep of an abandoned warehouse flagged for suspected chemical stockpiles, he had walked directly into a corroded storage tank that ruptured on contact. The chemical exposure—later identified as a volatile organophosphate compound—filled his lungs and burned through his eyes and throat with an intensity that made him certain, in those first moments, that he was dying. The sensation of drowning in air, of his body turning against itself, had been absolute. He had been hospitalized for six weeks.

The physical damage had resolved, more or less. But something in Kofi's mind had not.

Fourteen years later, at sixty-two, he had come to believe that his body remained fundamentally compromised, that the toxins had lodged somewhere in his cells and were waiting for the right trigger—the wrong smell, the wrong exertion, the wrong moment of vulnerability—to finish what they had started. This fear had become the architecture of his daily life. At work, where he still insisted on being assigned to jobs despite the repeated suggestions from his supervisor that he transition to training or administrative roles, he had developed an elaborate system of escape routes. Before entering any building, he mapped exits: doors, windows, the location of the nearest external wall. If he could not identify a clear path out, he would not enter. His colleagues had stopped commenting on it. On jobs, his hypervigilance had become so pronounced that he would interrupt his own work to scan the perimeter for signs of danger—a shift in the light, an unusual sound, anything that might signal a release of fumes or a structural failure. He had become slower, more deliberate, but also exhausted in a way that no amount of sleep seemed to address.

The loudness of the detonation simulator during training exercises—the controlled explosions that were part of his job—had begun to trigger a startle response so acute that his hands would shake for hours afterward. The sound carried him back to that warehouse, to the moment of rupture, to the sensation of poison entering his body. Sirens from ambulances passing near the station made his chest tighten. He had started to avoid hospitals entirely, which meant that when his wife, Ama, had urged him to see a cardiologist about palpitations he had been experiencing, he had refused. The thought of walking into a hospital, of encountering the smell of antiseptic that would inevitably trigger a cascade of memories and physical sensations, was intolerable. He had not had a physical examination in six years.

To manage the thoughts that came when he was still—the intrusive replaying of those moments in the warehouse, the certainty that his body was failing—Kofi had thrown himself into work. He volunteered for extra shifts, took on administrative tasks he disliked, stayed at the station late into the evenings. The irony was not lost on him: the workplace that contained his most potent triggers had also become his refuge from the thoughts that threatened him when alone. At home, he found reasons to remain occupied. He had begun to avoid sitting in rooms with closed doors, and he had developed a pattern of leaving the house early and returning late, which had created a growing distance between him and Ama. She had stopped asking him to sit with her in the evenings. The isolation he was fleeing had come to define his marriage.

When someone at work had touched his shoulder unexpectedly last month—a colleague simply trying to get his attention—Kofi had nearly struck him, his body reacting with an alarm that felt entirely beyond his control. The shock on his colleague's face, the realization that he was no longer entirely safe to be around, had finally broken something in him. At sixty-two, after fourteen years of managing alone, Kofi had made an appointment with a therapist. He was terrified of what exploring these fears might mean, but more terrified still of the man he was becoming.
